title: Factors & Divisor Counting
coreInsight: Choosing a divisor means independently choosing how many copies of each prime factor to include, so divisor counts arise from multiplying exponent-choice counts.
targetLearnerRealization: Every divisor corresponds to an independent choice of prime exponent from 0 up to the exponent available in the number.
learningObjectives: Construct every positive divisor from allowed prime exponents.
Explain why exponent zero includes 1 and why full exponents include the number itself.
Derive and use the divisor-count formula by multiplying independent choice counts.
Apply exponent constraints to count selected kinds of divisors without duplication.

continuity.openingCallback: Turn a prime inventory into all smaller inventories that its available prime copies can build.
closingSeeds: Restrictions such as odd, square, or divisible by a fixed number become restrictions on exponent choices.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Only factor pairs need to be counted.
1 and the number itself can be omitted.
Exponent-choice counts should be added rather than multiplied.
Different construction orders create different divisors.

beats.purpose: Discover divisors as all independent exponent choices for 72.
beats.expectedRealization: Four choices for the exponent of 2 and three for the exponent of 3 fill a 12-cell grid of distinct divisors.
beats.transitionIn: A prime factorization records every available tile. Instead of using all the tiles, choose any allowed number of each kind and inspect the products.
beats.transitionOut: The completed grid contains every divisor exactly once, so 4 × 3 gives 12 divisors.
beats.whyNow: A complete grid makes both coverage and the product rule visible before a formula is named.
beats.entryBridge: Use 72 = 2³ × 3². Let the exponent of 2 range from 0 to 3 and the exponent of 3 from 0 to 2.
beats.exitBridge: Each row-column intersection fixes one exponent pair and therefore one product.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A Cartesian grid indexed by prime exponents.
learnerPrompts: How many choices are available in each prime column?
Can two different cells produce the same divisor?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count exponent choices including zero, then pair every 2-exponent with every 3-exponent.

visual.ariaLabel: Twelve divisors of seventy-two arranged by exponents of two and three

steps.body: Each cell has the form 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ with 0 ≤ a ≤ 3 and 0 ≤ b ≤ 2.
Unique prime factorization means two different exponent pairs cannot create the same positive integer.

resolution.takeaway: Every divisor is one exponent-choice tuple, and every allowed tuple is one divisor.

beats.purpose: Explain the boundary exponent choices and retain 1 and the number itself.
beats.expectedRealization: Choosing exponent zero for every prime gives 1; choosing every full exponent gives the original number.
beats.transitionIn: Inspect the opposite corners of the divisor grid.
beats.prompt: Which statement explains why both 1 and 72 belong in the grid?

options.text: 2⁰ × 3⁰ = 1, while 2³ × 3² = 72.
Endpoints are usually omitted from divisor counts.
One is included because it is prime.
Seventy-two is included only as an extra special case.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—both arise naturally from allowed exponent choices.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Exponent zero means choosing no copies of that prime, and the full exponent means choosing every available copy.

steps.body: Choosing zero copies of both primes gives the empty product 1. Choosing all three 2s and both 3s reconstructs 72.

resolution.takeaway: The exponent ranges include both endpoints, so the divisor list includes 1 and the number itself.

beats.purpose: Prove the grid is exhaustive and nonduplicating rather than merely a list of examples.
beats.expectedRealization: Any divisor of 72 can use no other primes and cannot exceed the available exponents; unique factorization prevents duplicates.
beats.transitionIn: A useful counting grid must prove that nothing is missing and nothing is counted twice.
beats.prompt: Why does the 4-by-3 grid contain every positive divisor of 72 exactly once?

options.text: A divisor can use only 2ᵃ3ᵇ within the available bounds, and unique prime factorization gives one exponent pair per value.
Every divisor must be the smaller member of a factor pair.
Choosing 2s before 3s makes a new divisor.
Twelve examples are enough to prove completeness.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—allowed bounds prove coverage; unique prime factorization proves non-overlap.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Factor a supposed divisor into primes and compare its exponents with those available in 72.

steps.body: If d divides 72, the prime factors of d must come from 2³ × 3², so d = 2ᵃ3ᵇ within the grid bounds.
One integer cannot have two different prime exponent lists, so no two cells duplicate a divisor.

resolution.takeaway: Coverage plus uniqueness turns the grid into a proof, not a sample.

beats.purpose: Derive multiplication rather than addition for independent exponent choices.
beats.expectedRealization: Each of four 2-exponent choices pairs with each of three 3-exponent choices.
beats.transitionIn: Count the grid without listing its cell values.
beats.prompt: Why are the choice counts multiplied as 4 × 3 rather than added as 4 + 3?

options.text: Every choice for the exponent of 2 can be paired with every choice for the exponent of 3.
A divisor chooses either a power of 2 or a power of 3, but not both.
Multiplication is used only because it gives a bigger answer.
Divisors always come in exactly four factor pairs.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—one choice from each independent column forms a complete exponent tuple.
beats.incorrectFeedback: For each of the four column choices, count all three row choices.

steps.body: There are three cells for each of four 2-exponent choices: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.

beats.purpose: Name the divisor-count rule after its grid proof.
beats.expectedRealization: For n = p₁^a₁⋯pₖ^aₖ, each exponent offers aᵢ+1 choices, whose product counts divisors.
beats.transitionIn: The grid dimensions generalize to any number of distinct prime columns.
beats.name: Divisor-count formula
beats.conciseDefinition: If n = p₁^a₁p₂^a₂⋯pₖ^aₖ, then n has (a₁+1)(a₂+1)⋯(aₖ+1) positive divisors.
beats.memoryHook: Include exponent zero, then multiply the choice counts.

beats.purpose: Connect complete divisor counting with factor-pair intuition without losing square endpoints.
beats.expectedRealization: Factor pairs can check a list, but divisor count refers to individual divisors and squares have a repeated middle pair.
beats.transitionIn: Factor pairs are a useful check, but they package two divisors at a time and need care at a square root.
beats.prompt: Seventy-two has 12 divisors. How many unordered factor pairs does it have?
beats.correctFeedback: Right—the 12 divisors pair across products equal to 72, giving 6 pairs.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Pair the smallest unused divisor with 72 divided by it.

resolution.takeaway: Count divisors as values; use factor pairs only as an organized cross-check.

beats.purpose: Extend divisor construction into a bounded enumeration of increasing factor triples.
beats.expectedRealization: Prime tiles of 100 can be distributed into three ordered boxes in exactly four strictly increasing ways.
beats.transitionIn: Instead of placing selected prime copies into one divisor box, distribute all four prime copies of 100 among three boxes whose products must increase.
beats.transitionOut: Bounding the smallest factor made the enumeration complete and left four triples.
beats.whyNow: The approved additional problem uses the same exponent inventory while demanding a systematic, nonduplicating multi-factor search.
beats.entryBridge: Use 100 = 2² × 5² and first bound the smallest factor below the cube root of 100.
beats.exitBridge: The surviving triples redistribute the same prime tiles: (1,2,50), (1,4,25), (1,5,20), and (2,5,10).
beats.reusedRepresentation: Prime tokens distributed among factor boxes.
learnerPrompts: Why must a be below the cube root of 100?
For each possible a, what interval can contain b?
How does strict order prevent duplicate arrangements?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—there are four strictly increasing triples.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Restrict a to divisors below ∛100, then for each a require a < b < √(100/a).

steps.body: Because a < b < c, we have a³ < abc = 100, so a can only be 1, 2, or 4 among the divisors.
Testing the bounded b-window gives three triples for a = 1, one for a = 2, and none for a = 4.

resolution.takeaway: Bounds and strict order make a multiplicative enumeration complete without recounting permutations.

beats.purpose: Repair duplicate counting caused by construction order.
beats.expectedRealization: Selecting exponent 2 then exponent 3 or reversing the mental order produces the same tuple and divisor.
beats.transitionIn: Return from three boxes to one divisor cell and separate choices from the order in which they were considered.
beats.prompt: A divisor uses 2² and 3¹. Does choosing the 2-exponent first versus the 3-exponent first create two divisors?

options.text: No. Both routes specify the same exponent pair and the same divisor 12.
Yes. Different choice order always creates a new divisor.
Yes, so every divisor should be multiplied by 2!.
No, because 12 is not a divisor of 72.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the tuple is the object being counted, not the sequence used to select it.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiplication is commutative: 2² × 3 and 3 × 2² are both 12.

steps.body: The grid cell is indexed by the final pair (a,b). A route to the cell does not create another cell.

resolution.takeaway: Count completed exponent tuples, not construction histories.

beats.purpose: Count all divisors of 2020 and classify which divisors themselves have more than three divisors.
beats.expectedRealization: The 3 × 2 × 2 exponent box contains 12 divisors; exactly five have at most three divisors, leaving seven.
beats.transitionIn: A larger exponent box now asks a second divisor-count question inside each cell.
beats.transitionOut: Twelve total cells minus the five single-prime-axis cells leaves seven qualifying factors.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer layers the divisor-count formula onto its own generated divisors after the grid model is secure.
beats.entryBridge: Factor 2020, generate its exponent box, then use each cell's exponents to count that cell's divisors.
beats.exitBridge: Any cell using two distinct primes already has at least 2 × 2 = 4 divisors.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A Cartesian grid of allowed prime exponents, each cell representing one divisor.
learnerPrompts: How many cells are in the exponent box?
Which cells have divisor count at most 3?
Why do all remaining cells qualify?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—7 factors of 2020 have more than 3 factors.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 2020 = 2² × 5 × 101 for 12 total divisors, then remove 1, 2, 4, 5, and 101.

steps.body: The divisors with at most three divisors are 1, 2, 4, 5, and 101.
Thus 12 − 5 = 7 divisors have more than three divisors.

resolution.takeaway: Exponent grids can support a second structural filter without listing candidates at random.

beats.transitionIn: Build the grid dimensions without drawing every cell.
beats.transitionOut: Three independent exponent ranges multiply to 18 choices.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks the core technique independently.
beats.entryBridge: Factor first, then include exponent zero in each range.
learnerPrompts: How many choices does each allow?

steps.body: The allowed exponents number 3, 3, and 2, so d(180) = (2+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 18.

resolution.takeaway: Add one to each prime exponent, then multiply.

beats.purpose: Assess endpoint inclusion for a prime power.
beats.expectedRealization: The divisors of 2⁶ use exponents 0 through 6, giving seven divisors.
beats.transitionIn: Collapse the grid to a single prime axis and retain both endpoints.
beats.transitionOut: The seven exponent choices generate 1 through 64 as powers of 2.
beats.whyNow: A near item isolates the +1 in the formula.
beats.entryBridge: List allowed exponents, not factor pairs.
learnerPrompts: What do the endpoint choices build?

steps.body: Every divisor is 2ᵃ for exactly one a from 0 through 6. That gives 7 divisors.

resolution.takeaway: A prime power pᵃ has a+1 positive divisors.

beats.expectedRealization: Eight divisors of 360 are divisible by 12.
beats.transitionIn: Restrict the exponent box to cells that contain a required sub-inventory.
beats.transitionOut: The lower bounds from 12 leave 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cells.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item turns a divisibility condition into exponent-range restrictions.
beats.exitBridge: Count allowed choices only after applying lower and upper bounds.
learnerPrompts: What minimum exponents does divisibility by 12 require?
How many allowed values remain for each exponent?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—8 divisors of 360 are multiples of 12.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Choose the exponent of 2 from {2,3}, of 3 from {1,2}, and of 5 from {0,1}.

steps.body: A divisor of 360 has exponents a∈{0,1,2,3}, b∈{0,1,2}, c∈{0,1}. Divisibility by 12 = 2² × 3 requires a≥2 and b≥1.
The remaining choices number 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

resolution.takeaway: Conditions carve a smaller rectangular region from the exponent-choice box.

beats.purpose: Assess fixing one exponent under a parity constraint.
beats.expectedRealization: Odd divisors of 840 must use exponent zero for 2, leaving 2³ = 8 choices for the odd primes.
beats.transitionIn: A parity condition fixes one coordinate instead of merely shortening its range.
beats.transitionOut: Setting the 2-exponent to zero leaves independent binary choices for 3, 5, and 7.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item links divisibility meaning to constrained counting.
beats.entryBridge: Factor 840 and decide what oddness requires of the 2-exponent.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 840 = 2³ × 3 × 5 × 7 and force the exponent of 2 to be 0.

steps.body: An odd divisor contains no factor 2, so its 2-exponent is fixed at 0. Each of 3, 5, and 7 may have exponent 0 or 1.
Thus there are 1 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 odd divisors.

resolution.takeaway: Fix constrained exponents, then multiply choices for the free coordinates.

beats.purpose: Assess multi-coordinate parity constraints on divisor exponents.
beats.expectedRealization: A square divisor uses only even exponents, giving 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 choices.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, restrict every coordinate by a perfect-square condition.
beats.transitionOut: Even exponent choices in the three columns multiply to 12 square divisors.
beats.whyNow: The challenge composes exponent ranges, parity, and independent counting.
beats.entryBridge: A perfect square has even exponents in its prime factorization.
beats.exitBridge: Each exponent tuple remains unique, so no construction-order correction is needed.
learnerPrompts: Which even exponents are allowed in each column?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use exponents {0,2,4} for 2 and {0,2} for both 3 and 5.

steps.body: For 2⁵ × 3³ × 5², square divisors allow 2-exponents 0,2,4; 3-exponents 0,2; and 5-exponents 0,2.
The number of tuples is 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.

resolution.takeaway: Property constraints become allowed-exponent sets whose sizes multiply.

beats.purpose: Consolidate coverage, uniqueness, endpoints, and multiplication.
beats.expectedRealization: The divisor formula counts unique complete exponent tuples over inclusive ranges.
beats.transitionIn: Every successful count used the same proof structure, even when conditions removed cells.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable divisor count? Select all four.

options.text: Prime-factor the original number completely.
Include exponent 0 in every allowed range.
Multiply independent exponent-choice counts.
Count each completed exponent tuple once, regardless of construction order.
Omit 1 and the original number.

response.feedback: Factor, include zero, multiply independent choices, and count tuples once.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—those checks establish both the formula and its correct use.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Exponent zero and the full exponents naturally include 1 and the number.

resolution.takeaway: Divisors are unique exponent choices from inclusive, independent ranges.

beats.purpose: Connect divisor counting to general constrained product-space reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: Many special-divisor questions are ordinary exponent grids with coordinates fixed or restricted.
beats.transitionIn: Odd, square, and required-factor conditions changed only which exponent values were allowed.
beats.prompt: When a problem asks for divisors with an extra property, how can you translate that property into allowed exponent choices before counting?
beats.takeaway: Describe the allowed exponent set in each prime column; then multiply the remaining independent choices.

The approved 2022 problem is guided enumeration and the approved 2020 problem is the mapped advanced transfer.
